Reading some of the other posts about people's success stories, thought I'd share mine.

Background

I have dabbled in Linux for over 15 years. I've gone down such roads as compiling my entire distro (Gentoo), running Mandrake, RedHat, FreeBSD (and variants), Debian and more. I always ran into some quirky driver issue and found myself having to compile custom kernels to get it to work. Eventually, I would get frustrated at not being able to simply "do" things like I could with my knowledge of Windows, so I would go back.

Like many others, Windows 10 pushed me over. I hated all the background garbage that was running in the OS that I couldn't uninstall or turn off. (XBox tiles and the like ...) I wanted more control over what my OS was doing. That, and other quirks were adding up: Having to hit the keyboard several times to "wake up" windows, file copy operations taking MUCH longer than they should, etc.

First Computer: Desktop

I am the kind of person that will do something over and over until I get it just right. I decided to give Ubuntu a try on my main desktop. Added some more HDDs and dual-booted. I setup full-disk encryption (more about that later) and went to work customizing it. In the process of jumping between window managers, I broke some stuff (probably repairable, but the time to find out how surpassed simply starting over), so I re-installed again. And again. I tweaked Unity to my liking, but the Amazon integration and such felt too invasive. Since I wanted to stay bleeding-edge, I installed the latest version (15.10) of Ubu, and it works well. Except for stuff that is compiled against older versions (I still can't get WINE to work...) But, for my desktop, it works "good enough". After a few weeks of running it as my primary OS, I wiped my windows HDD (after copying over personal files) and relished in my new-found freedom from Microsoft.

I ran into some permissioning issues with my Plex media server--and had to change the mount options for one of my HDDs so Plex could read it. In the end, I found articles to show me how, and now that works great.

Hardware:

AMD Phenum II X4 965 CPU, NVidia GeForce GTX 560 Ti video card, 16 GB RAM

Second Machine: Laptop

I initially installed Ubuntu on this one as well, and after some time decided to give Mint a try (with Cinnamon). I personally didn't like it too much and switched back to Ubuntu. Then, I started watching reviews of different flavors of Mint, and decided that I wanted a machine where things "just worked". So, I installed Mint MATE and freakin' LOVE IT. Sure, the kernel is a little older, but everything just works. WINE, apps, Steam, all of it. Oh, and compiz. Compiz is freaking great.

Again, I setup full-disk encryption using LUKS. This time around, I decided I wanted to try and customize my partitions a bit (/boot is too small IMHO using default setups, and I hate running out of room on it with kernel updates...). Holy crap, this was a nightmare. Full disk encryption with custom partitioning is a pain and in the end, I couldn't get it to work. :( This is an area that needs some work with Linux Mint. So, I went back to the default partitioning and occasionally have to clean-up /boot.

I setup VirtualBox to run Windows Server 2012 as a work machine (MUCH better than Windows 8.1/10--none of the bloat and crap) and it runs faster than the physical Microsoft Surface Pro 3 my company provided me.

Drivers for everything just work (with the exception of the proprietary fingerprint reader, but I don't need that). Multi-finger gestures on my trackpad, WiFi, bluetooth, camera, etc.

Hardware:

Lenovo ThinkPad T440s. Intel i7-4600U, 12 GB RAM, 1920 x 1080 display, 3 freakin' SSDs, 2 batteries. This laptop is awesome. 14", not too big, easy to carry around. Yes, I have 3 SSDs in it--with the M.2 ports, it is possible. Between the internal battery and the external extended-capacity battery, I get 10+ hours of battery life, no problem. This thing is a beast.

Conclusion

I run Linux 100% on my personal machines now and love it. I don't miss Microsoft, and most of my Steam games play just fine. If you are a gamer, you don't even need to dual-boot. This guy shows how you can get 95% native performance with Qemu/KVM under Linux.

I have an older friend who is computer-dumb (took him a while to grasp single-clicking vs double-clicking)--and I installed Linux Mint MATE on his machine and he LOVES it. If he can use it in his day-to-day computing, anyone can.

Thanks for reading, and thank you all for your support. This is a great community.
